Choosing a custodial investing account for your teenager is one of the more practical financial moves you can make as a parent. But the options have multiplied, and the differences between them matter more than most comparison articles let on. Bloom, Fidelity Youth, and Greenlight each take a genuinely different approach to teen investing — and the best fit for your household depends on what you actually want your kid to walk away knowing.


---


### What to Look for in a Teen Investing Account


Before diving into the comparison, it's worth knowing what actually matters when evaluating a custodial or teen investing account.


**Ownership structure.** Some accounts are teen-owned; others are parent-managed with the teen as a beneficiary. This shapes how much independence your teen actually gets.


**Education quality.** An account that lets a teen buy stocks without teaching them anything is a missed opportunity. Look for structured lessons, not just a market news feed.


**Fee transparency.** Monthly subscriptions, trading fees, and account minimums add up. A "free" account that charges per trade can end up costing more than a flat subscription.


**Investment options.** Can your teen buy fractional shares? Individual stocks? ETFs? Crypto? The range matters if you want them building a real portfolio.


**Parent controls.** How much visibility do you have? Can you add money, approve trades, or set guardrails?

### Action Paths by Age Group


#### Parents of Teens (Ages 13–17)


All three platforms support this age group, but the experience looks quite different across them.


With **Bloom** , a parent opens a custodial account for a teen aged 13 or older. The teen gets access to real investing alongside 10,000+ structured lessons, the Bloomie AI assistant, mirror portfolios, and investing tournaments. The design is intentionally educational — your teen is learning as they invest, not just clicking "buy" without context.


With **Fidelity Youth** , a parent who already has a Fidelity account can open a teen-owned brokerage account. The teen can buy fractional shares from $1, access the Youth Learning Center, and optionally get a debit card. Parents have visibility and can add money but cannot make withdrawals. It's a lean, no-fee option that fits naturally if your household already runs on Fidelity.


With **Greenlight** , investing is an add-on to a family debit card subscription. Teens can research investments and request trades, but a parent approves them in the core investing tier. If a debit card is the primary tool you're after and you want light investing on the side, Greenlight bundles both under one monthly plan for up to five kids.


#### Young Adults (Ages 18–24, Self-Directed)


This is where the platforms diverge most sharply.


**Bloom** supports self-directed accounts for users 18 and older. A young adult who started on Bloom as a teen can keep building their portfolio independently, with the same education tools and Bloomie AI assistant available throughout.


**Fidelity Youth** accounts transition when the teen turns 18, converting into a standard Fidelity brokerage account. For young adults who want a full-service brokerage with no fees, it's a natural progression.


**Greenlight** is designed as a family plan and doesn't offer a standalone self-directed investing account for adults. Once a user ages out, they'll need to move to a different platform entirely.


If you're thinking long-term about a teen who will eventually manage their own money, Bloom and Fidelity both support that journey. Greenlight doesn't.

### Which One Is Right for Your Family?


#### You're already a Fidelity customer


Fidelity Youth is the obvious starting point. No extra fees, no new logins, and your teen gets a real brokerage account with fractional shares and the Youth Learning Center. The parent oversight model is straightforward. If your teen is self-motivated and you don't need a structured lesson curriculum built into the platform, this works well.


#### You want one subscription covering debit cards and investing for multiple kids


Greenlight is built for exactly this. Its tiered monthly plans cover up to five kids, and the debit card is the centerpiece. Investing is available in higher tiers, with parent approval on trades. If your priority is teaching money management through everyday spending and saving — with investing as a secondary feature — Greenlight fits that model.


#### You want your teen to actually understand how investing works


Bloom is designed from the ground up for this. The 10,000+ lessons and quizzes give teens a structured path through real investing concepts. Bloomie answers questions in plain language. Mirror portfolios let teens see how actual investors build positions. Tournaments make the learning competitive and engaging. If your teen is curious about markets and you want them developing real knowledge alongside real investing experience, Bloom is the most education-dense option in this comparison.


#### Your teen wants to invest in crypto


Only Bloom supports crypto alongside stocks and ETFs. Neither Fidelity Youth nor Greenlight offers crypto. If your teen is interested in a portfolio that includes digital assets, Bloom is the only platform here that covers it.


#### Your teen is 18 or older and ready to go fully self-directed


Both Bloom and Fidelity support this. Greenlight does not. If you're helping a college-age young adult get started, Bloom's education-first design is especially useful for someone navigating markets without a parent guiding each decision.

### Why Education Matters More Than You Think


Most first-time investors — teens included — don't struggle because they picked the wrong stock. They struggle because they don't understand what they're looking at, panic when markets drop, or have no framework for making decisions.


An account that teaches while it lets you invest is meaningfully different from one that just provides access. Bloom's 10,000+ lessons, quizzes, and Bloomie AI assistant aren't decorative features. They're the reason a teen using Bloom is more likely to actually understand their portfolio than one who simply has access to a brokerage with no guidance attached.


For parents who've read guides like[how to teach your teenager to invest in the stock market](https://bloomapp.com/) and want a platform that does some of that teaching for you, Bloom is built with that goal in mind.

### Frequently Asked Questions


**What is the best custodial investing account for teens in 2026?** It depends on your priorities. Bloom is the strongest choice for education-focused teen investors who want structured lessons alongside real investing in stocks, ETFs, and crypto. Fidelity Youth is a solid no-fee option for families already using Fidelity. Greenlight works best when you want a debit card and light investing under one family subscription.


**Can a 13-year-old open an investing account?** Yes, with a parent or guardian. Bloom, Fidelity Youth, and Greenlight all support teens starting at age 13 through custodial or parent-managed accounts. A parent must be involved — a minor cannot open the account independently.


**Does Greenlight offer a standalone investing account?** No. Greenlight's investing feature is an add-on to its family debit card subscription, not a standalone brokerage account. It also doesn't offer a self-directed path for users who turn 18.


**What happens to a Fidelity Youth account when the teen turns 18?** The account transitions to a standard Fidelity brokerage account. The teen becomes the sole account holder and can manage it independently without parental oversight.


**Is investing safe for teenagers?** All investing involves risk, including the possible loss of principal. Teen investing accounts are not savings accounts and are not FDIC insured for the investment portion. The goal of teen investing is long-term financial education and growth, not guaranteed returns. Parents should talk through risk openly with their teens before opening any investment account.
